title: Some teens are now AI vegans
author: Mike Taubman
summary: High school teacher Mike Taubman describes noticing a new stance among his students: AI vegans, who abstain from AI for environmental, personal, or moral reasons. He respects their reasons but notes that today's students will graduate into a world requiring them to be intellectual and technical omnivores. In his career-connected learning program he has taken two approaches. He makes AI ambient, offering a customized AI assistant that can stand in as an expert for students' varied projects while teaching that AI should be subordinate to their own vision, which he believes defangs the AI bogeyman. He also makes AI optional, pointing out its strange and unnerving behavior and letting students choose whether to use it, to build agency. Taubman closes with open questions about dependency and preparation, concluding that teachers must both look ahead for students and listen to what students see.
points: Taubman first sensed AI veganism in an 11th grader's tone when she declared she does not use AI.
He customizes a privacy-protected AI assistant for each class session to act as a stand-in career expert.
Fewer than half of his students used the available AI assistant during one project work session.
He points out AI oddities, such as an image generator giving a robot human family members, to foster critical use.
He frames his role as giving students the menu and taking their order on whether to use AI.
quotes: When I introduced AI for 26-27, an 11th grader said some version of “I don’t use AI.” It wasn’t so much what she said but how she said it. For her, this was a moral stance.

Unlike the original vegans, today’s high schoolers are graduating into a world that will require them to be intellectual and technical omnivores, capable of critical engagement with AI as both a tool and a topic.
That, I said, is what it looks like to use AI as an assistant. It should be subordinate to your own personal vision, not providing that vision for you.

Part of my evolving thinking here is that when I say AI is available and provide direct instruction about how to use it, and then treat it as just another resource students can consult, it defangs the AI bogeyman.
Normalizing appropriate AI use does not mean normalizing AI.
The point is the authentic choice. I see my job as giving students the menu and then taking their order.
But another one of our jobs is to listen to what students say they’re seeing, because they will spend more time over that horizon than we will.
